analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal agency to screen and mediate asbestos injury claims, barring lawsuits that fail its medical criteria and banning punitive damages.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 105th Congress, the bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and died there in January 1999 without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have moved asbestos injury claims out of the ordinary court system and into a new federal Asbestos Resolution Corporation. Sick workers would first need a certificate of medical eligibility from the Corporation, then go through mandatory mediation before they could sue or choose arbitration. It would ban punitive damages, block class actions unless every defendant agreed, cap attorneys' fees, and set strict medical criteria a claimant must meet. In exchange, it would erase statutes of limitations as a defense and impose a penalty on companies that make lowball settlement offers.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing asbestos lawsuits and their insurers would gain the most: fewer claims would qualify, punitive damages would be gone, collective lawsuits would require their consent, and the system's costs would be spread among them in advance. Seriously ill claimants with qualifying diseases would gain a faster, guaranteed route to compensation that no company could delay with time-limit defenses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asbestos manufacturers, insurers, and very sick claimants

how_it_helps.text: Claimants who qualify medically could no longer be blocked by statutes of limitations or repose defenses, which currently force workers to sue before they are sick to preserve their rights [S3].

Seriously ill claimants would get a structured path: a medical eligibility decision within roughly 90 days, mandatory mediation, then a choice of arbitration or court, with a 10% penalty added to awards against defendants whose final settlement offers fall below 75% of the eventual award [S3].

The bill requires cost shares to be allocated proportionally among the prior year's respondents and funds the system through a dedicated trust fund, so no taxpayer money pays for claim processing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Asbestos defendant companies would fund the medical review system and bear litigation and arbitration costs, but their total payouts would likely fall because punitive damages are banned, claims by people without qualifying impairment are screened out, class actions are barred, and attorneys' fees are capped. Workers with real exposure whose conditions do not meet the strict medical criteria would lose any recovery at all, and plaintiffs' lawyers would lose fee income.

drawbacks.text: The medical criteria are narrow and objective: nonmalignant claimants must meet specific x-ray, breathing-test, and lung-capacity thresholds, and lung cancer claimants generally need either a qualifying nonmalignant condition or documented pleural changes plus 15 counted years of exposure, with exposure years after 1979 largely not counted [S3]. Workers genuinely exposed but below those thresholds would be barred from any court recovery.
Punitive damages would be banned outright in every asbestos case, removing the main legal tool for punishing and deterring companies that hid asbestos hazards [S3].
No class action, joinder, or consolidation of claims would be allowed without each defendant's consent, forcing thousands of similar cases to be tried one at a time [S3].
Attorneys' fees would be capped by federal law regardless of any contingency contract, reducing the practical availability of legal representation for individual claimants [S2].
The bill would preempt state courts' handling of asbestos claims, including pending cases not yet reduced to final judgment [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine trade rather than a pure giveaway: it would guarantee seriously ill workers a prompt, delay-proof compensation route and make defendants pay for the system, and its drafters could point to a tort system where less than half of asbestos litigation costs reach claimants. But the price is steep and falls on the workers: strict federal medical screens would cut off many exposed people entirely, punitive deterrence disappears, and collective litigation ends. On balance, the biggest sure winners are the defendant companies, which is why the bill reads mainly as liability relief for industry with a compensation guarantee attached.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the closing weeks of the session and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on October 2, 1998, with five cosponsors [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor action followed [S5].
The cosponsor list showed early bipartisan support: three Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with the Judiciary Committee never voting on it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the existing court system stayed in place. Plaintiffs' attorneys and asbestos claimants kept the current tort system, and defendant companies kept facing suits but avoided the bill's new mandatory funding and cost-allocation duties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trial lawyers and claimants kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: a Republican lead sponsor with three Democratic and two Republican cosponsors, and no recorded floor opposition because the bill never advanced past committee.

industries.industry: Asbestos defendant manufacturers and their insurers
industries.note: The bill would screen out claims that fail strict medical criteria, ban punitive damages, and require defendant consent for class actions, cutting total payouts. In exchange, defendants would fund the medical review system and face a penalty for lowball settlement offers, and seriously ill claimants would get a guaranteed, delay-proof path to payment.

Federal fee caps, mandatory pre-suit screening, and a ban on collective handling of claims would sharply reduce contingency fee volume. Claimants would lose some recovery alongside their lawyers, since punitive damages and many impairment claims would be barred.
